title: Pickle Juice for a Hangover: Does It Work? How Much to Drink
excerpt: Does pickle juice help a hangover? What the sodium in brine can and can't do, the muscle-cramp research, how much to drink, pickleback shots, and who should skip it.
metaDescription: Does pickle juice help a hangover? What the sodium in brine can and can't fix, how much to drink, pickleback shots, and who should skip it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** pickle juice can help a little with one specific part of a hangover, which is the salt and fluid you lose from drinking, sweating, and especially vomiting. A small glass of brine gives you a quick hit of sodium, and sodium helps your body hold on to the water you drink afterward. What pickle juice can't do is fix the rest of a hangover. There is no good evidence that it clears headaches, nausea, fatigue, or the foggy feeling, because those come mostly from inflammation, poor sleep, and the by-products of breaking down alcohol, not from low salt. Think of it as a salty rehydration helper, not a cure.

**The quick rules:** If you want to try it, sip 1 to 3 ounces (2 to 6 tablespoons) of dill pickle brine, then follow it with a large glass of plain water. Don't chug a whole jar. Skip it or keep it very small if you have high blood pressure, heart or kidney disease, are on a low-sodium diet, or are struggling with heartburn. A pickle or two with some food gives you roughly the same benefit with less of a jolt to your stomach.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover after a night out gets better on its own within a day. Get medical help if you **can't keep any fluids down for more than several hours, are vomiting repeatedly, see blood in your vomit, are barely urinating or your urine is very dark, feel confused, faint, or have a racing heart that won't settle.** Those are signs of real dehydration or something more serious, and a pickle-brine shot is not the right tool. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin after drinking, that can be alcohol poisoning: call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away and don't let them "sleep it off."

## Why People Drink Pickle Juice for a Hangover

Pickle brine as a hangover remedy is old. In Russia and much of Eastern Europe, drinking the brine from a jar of pickles (often called *rassol*) the morning after is a long-standing tradition, and similar habits show up wherever salty, sour fermented foods are common. In the US, the idea got a second life through two routes. Athletes started drinking pickle juice for muscle cramps, and bars made the "pickleback" (a shot of whiskey chased by a shot of brine) a fixture. Put those together and it's easy to see why people reach for the jar on a rough morning.

The logic people give is simple: alcohol dehydrates you, you lose electrolytes, and pickle juice is basically salt water with vinegar. That logic is partly right, and it's worth separating the part that holds up from the part that doesn't.

## What Is Actually in Pickle Juice?

Standard grocery-store dill pickle brine is mostly:

- **Water**, which is what you need most when you're dehydrated.
- **Sodium**, from salt. This is the main thing pickle juice brings to the table. Brine is very salty: even a couple of ounces typically contains several hundred milligrams of sodium, and some brands contain much more. The exact amount varies widely, so check the nutrition label on your jar (the sodium listed per pickle spear gives you a rough idea of how concentrated the brine is).
- **Vinegar (acetic acid)**, which makes it sour and acidic.
- **Small amounts of potassium**, depending on the recipe. Brine generally has far less potassium than sodium.
- **Flavorings** like dill, garlic, mustard seed, and sometimes sugar (sweet pickles and bread-and-butter pickles have a lot more sugar).
- **Sometimes dyes or preservatives**, depending on the brand.

There are also bottled "pickle juice" drinks sold specifically for athletes. These are essentially brine made to drink, sometimes with extra electrolytes. They work the same basic way as the brine from your jar, just with a known, consistent sodium content.

### Fermented vs. vinegar pickles

Most shelf-stable pickles in the grocery aisle are made with vinegar and heat-treated, which means they don't contain live bacteria. Refrigerated "fermented" or "naturally fermented" pickles are made with salt brine and bacteria, and they may contain live cultures. That gets people excited about probiotics, but there's no good evidence that a shot of fermented brine does anything meaningful for a hangover. If you prefer fermented pickles, enjoy them, but don't count on the cultures to help you recover from last night.

## How Alcohol Dehydrates You (and Where Salt Comes In)

To understand what pickle juice can and can't do, it helps to know how drinking drains your fluids.

Alcohol lowers the release of a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone, or ADH). Normally this hormone tells your kidneys to hold on to water. When alcohol turns it down, your kidneys let more water go, which is why you need the bathroom so often on a night out. On top of that, many people sweat in warm bars or while dancing, eat little, and drink few non-alcoholic fluids.

The biggest electrolyte losses come from **vomiting and diarrhea**, which pull out water along with sodium, potassium, and chloride. If your night ended with you being sick, your body really is short on salt and fluid, and replacing both helps. If you simply drank a bit too much and woke up thirsty, you're mostly short on water.

Here's where sodium matters. When you drink plain water after you've lost a lot of fluid, your body can't hold on to all of it, and some passes straight through. Sodium helps your body keep the water you drink in your bloodstream and tissues instead of sending it to your bladder. That's the same principle behind oral rehydration solutions and sports drinks. Pickle juice is a crude, salty version of that idea.

## Does Pickle Juice Actually Help a Hangover?

Here's the evidence-based picture, piece by piece.

### What it plausibly helps with

- **Thirst and mild dehydration.** Brine is mostly water, and the sodium helps you retain what you drink afterward. If you follow a small shot with a big glass of water, you'll probably rehydrate a bit more effectively than with water alone, especially after vomiting or heavy sweating.
- **Salt cravings.** Many people genuinely want something salty the morning after. A small amount of brine, a pickle, or salty broth answers that craving quickly.
- **Muscle cramps.** If you wake up with a calf cramp or tight muscles, pickle juice may help (see the next section for why this happens faster than you'd expect).

### What it probably doesn't help with

- **Headache.** Hangover headaches are linked to inflammation, disrupted sleep, and changes in blood vessels. Fixing mild dehydration can take the edge off, but salt alone isn't a headache treatment. Our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers what does help.
- **Nausea.** Concentrated, sour, salty liquid can make an upset stomach worse for some people.
- **Fatigue and brain fog.** These come mostly from poor-quality sleep and the body's inflammatory response to alcohol, not from sodium levels.
- **Anxiety, shakes, and a racing heart.** These have more to do with your nervous system rebounding after alcohol and with blood sugar swings. See our piece on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) for more.

### What the research says about hangovers and electrolytes

There are no good clinical trials testing pickle juice as a hangover treatment. What we do have is broader hangover research, and it doesn't support the idea that electrolytes are the main cause of how bad a hangover feels. Studies that measured blood electrolytes in hungover people have generally not found that sodium or potassium levels track hangover severity. Hangover researchers now point mainly to the immune system's inflammatory response, poor sleep, acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), and other compounds in drinks.

That's why no salty drink, whether it's pickle brine, Gatorade, or Pedialyte, reliably cures a hangover. They help with the dehydration slice of the problem. That slice is real, especially after vomiting, but it's only one part of it.

## The Pickle Juice and Muscle Cramp Research

The most-cited science on pickle juice comes from sports medicine, not hangover research. In a well-known 2010 study led by Kevin Miller and published in *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise*, researchers induced muscle cramps in dehydrated men using electrical stimulation. Cramps eased faster after drinking a small amount of pickle juice than after drinking water.

The interesting part is *how fast* it worked. The relief came within a couple of minutes, which is far too quick for the sodium to have been absorbed and spread through the body. Related work from the same research group found that drinking pickle juice didn't meaningfully change blood electrolyte levels in the short term. The leading explanation is a reflex: the sharp, sour taste of vinegar in the mouth and throat appears to trigger nerve signals that calm the over-firing muscle. In other words, it's probably the vinegar's taste doing the work, not the salt reaching your muscles.

What this means for a hangover:

- If you have an actual muscle cramp, a sip of pickle juice is a reasonable thing to try, and it's cheap.
- The cramp research does **not** show that pickle juice rehydrates you quickly or fixes electrolyte levels. The rehydration benefit comes slowly, from the water and sodium together, the same way any salty fluid works.
- A small amount was used in this kind of research, not a big glass. More isn't better.

## How Much Pickle Juice Should You Drink?

There is no official dose for hangovers. A sensible approach is:

- **1 to 3 ounces (about 2 to 6 tablespoons)** of dill pickle brine, sipped rather than gulped.
- **Followed by 12 to 16 ounces of water.** The water is the main event. The brine is there to help you hold on to it.
- **Once, maybe twice,** over the morning. Don't keep going back to the jar.

Keep an eye on total salt. US dietary guidelines advise most adults to stay under 2,300 mg of sodium a day. Because brine is so concentrated, a large glass could put you well past that in one go, on top of whatever salty breakfast you're planning. For a healthy person, one salty morning isn't dangerous, but there's no benefit in overdoing it, and drinking a lot of very salty liquid can make you thirstier and upset your stomach.

### A gentler option: eat the pickle

If straight brine is too much, eat one or two pickles alongside some food. You'll get some sodium and a little fluid, and food helps steady your blood sugar and settle your stomach. Pairing it with something like toast, crackers, or [eggs](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) makes a more complete recovery breakfast than brine on its own.

### Diluted pickle juice

Some people mix a couple of tablespoons of brine into a large glass of water. That gives you a mildly salty drink that's easier on the stomach and closer in strength to a sports drink, though it won't have the sugar or potassium that properly formulated rehydration drinks include.

## Pickle Juice vs. Other Hangover Drinks

Here's how brine stacks up against the other things people reach for:

| Drink | Main strengths | Main drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| **Pickle juice** | Very high sodium, cheap, already in your fridge, may help cramps | Little potassium, no sugar to aid absorption, acidic, easy to overdo salt |
| **Plain water** | The basic fix for dehydration, gentle on the stomach | Without any salt, more of it passes straight through after heavy fluid loss |
| **Oral rehydration solutions (like Pedialyte)** | Balanced sodium, potassium, and glucose designed for rehydration | Costs more, taste isn't for everyone |
| **Sports drinks (like Gatorade)** | Some sodium and sugar, easy to drink | Less sodium than rehydration solutions, often a lot of sugar |
| **Coconut water** | Natural potassium, mild taste | Relatively low in sodium |
| **Broth or bouillon** | Salty, warm, easy on the stomach, often comforting | Can be very salty, little potassium |

The key point: rehydration works best when sodium and a little sugar (glucose) come together, because glucose helps your gut absorb sodium and water. That's the science behind oral rehydration solutions. Pickle juice has the sodium but generally not the sugar or the balanced potassium, so it's a less complete option. For a side-by-side breakdown, see our guides on [Pedialyte vs. Gatorade for hangovers](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover), [electrolyte drinks for hangovers compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared), and [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).

If you're comparing options, a reasonable rule of thumb is: after vomiting or a lot of sweating, an oral rehydration solution is the most complete choice. For ordinary morning-after thirst, water plus a salty snack (a pickle counts) works fine.

## Pickleback Shots: Do They Prevent a Hangover?

A pickleback is a shot of whiskey followed by a shot of pickle brine. The brine cuts the burn of the whiskey and leaves a salty, sour finish, which is why it's popular. Some people believe the brine chaser prevents a hangover.

There's no good evidence that it does. A one-ounce chaser of brine doesn't offset the alcohol in the shot before it, and taking extra shots because "the pickle juice cancels it out" is a fast way to end up with a worse morning. If you like picklebacks, enjoy them for the taste. Just count them as drinks like any other, and alternate with water through the night.

## Drinking Pickle Juice Before Bed or Before Drinking

Some people take a shot of brine before going out or before bed to "get ahead" of the hangover.

- **Before drinking:** there's no good evidence it helps. A full meal before you drink does more, because food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Before bed:** a small amount of brine with a big glass of water may help you retain some of that water overnight. It won't change how much alcohol you drank or how well you sleep. If heartburn is an issue for you, an acidic drink right before lying down may make it worse.

The approach with the strongest evidence is still the plain one: pace your drinks, eat beforehand, and drink water alongside alcohol. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes into more detail, and our article on [when to take electrolytes around drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing.

## Who Should Skip Pickle Juice

Pickle brine is a high-sodium, acidic drink. That's fine for most healthy adults in small amounts, but some people should skip it or ask a doctor first:

- **People with high blood pressure.** A concentrated dose of sodium can raise blood pressure, and alcohol can affect it too.
- **People with heart failure or kidney disease,** or anyone told to limit sodium or fluids. Your body may not handle a big salt load well.
- **People taking medications affected by sodium or fluid balance,** such as some blood pressure medicines or diuretics. Ask your pharmacist if you're not sure.
- **People with acid reflux or heartburn.** Vinegar is acidic, and alcohol already loosens the valve between your stomach and esophagus. If your stomach is burning, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).
- **People with sensitive teeth or enamel erosion.** Acidic drinks can be hard on enamel. Rinse your mouth with water afterward and wait a while before brushing.
- **Anyone vomiting a lot.** If you can't keep things down, salty brine is likely to come right back up. Small sips of an oral rehydration solution are a better choice, and repeated vomiting is a reason to get medical help.

## A Simple Pickle-Juice Hangover Routine

If you want to give it a try, here's a practical, honest way to use it:

1. **Start with water.** Drink a glass of water as soon as you're up.
2. **Take a small shot of brine,** 1 to 3 ounces, if you feel thirsty, crampy, or crave salt.
3. **Follow it with another big glass of water** over the next 15 to 30 minutes.
4. **Eat something.** Pair your pickle with real food, especially if you skipped dinner. Eggs, toast, oatmeal, or a banana are all reasonable.
5. **Rest.** Sleep is one of the biggest factors in how fast you recover, and no drink replaces it.
6. **Use a pain reliever carefully** if you need one, following the label and avoiding doubling up. Each painkiller has its own issues after drinking.
7. **Switch to a proper rehydration drink** if you were sick overnight or still feel very dry by midday.

If you're feeling worse instead of better as the day goes on, especially if you can't keep fluids down, go back to the "when to see a doctor" box at the top of this page.

## Where DHM Fits In

Pickle juice is a morning-after tool for the dehydration part of a hangover. Some people also look at what they can do the night before. One option people ask about is DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol.

Here's the honest picture: most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright. It also isn't a substitute for drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated. If you want to try it alongside sensible habits, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Pickle juice is a reasonable, cheap way to get some sodium back the morning after drinking, and sodium helps your body keep the water you drink. It's most useful if you sweated a lot or were sick, and it may ease a muscle cramp quickly thanks to a reflex triggered by its sour taste. It doesn't treat headaches, nausea, or fatigue, and there's no good evidence that it prevents or cures a hangover.

Keep the dose small (1 to 3 ounces), always follow it with plenty of water, and pair it with food. If you have high blood pressure, heart or kidney problems, or heartburn, skip it or ask your doctor. And if you can't keep fluids down or feel confused, faint, or very unwell, get medical help rather than reaching for the jar.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does pickle juice help a hangover?**

It can help a little with dehydration. Pickle brine is high in sodium, and sodium helps your body hold on to the water you drink, which is most useful if you sweated a lot or vomited. It does not treat the headache, nausea, or fatigue of a hangover, and there is no good evidence that it cures or prevents one. Treat it as a salty rehydration helper and follow it with plenty of water.

**How much pickle juice should I drink for a hangover?**

There is no official dose. A sensible amount is 1 to 3 ounces (about 2 to 6 tablespoons), sipped, then followed by a large glass of water. Brine is very salty, and US dietary guidelines advise most adults to stay under 2,300 mg of sodium a day, so drinking a whole glass or jar is more salt than you need.

**Is pickle juice better than Gatorade or Pedialyte for a hangover?**

Not really. Pickle juice has more sodium than most sports drinks but little potassium and usually no sugar, and a small amount of sugar helps your gut absorb sodium and water. Oral rehydration solutions like Pedialyte are designed with that balance, so they are the more complete choice after vomiting or heavy sweating. For ordinary morning-after thirst, water plus a salty snack works fine.

**Why does pickle juice help muscle cramps?**

In a 2010 study published in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, cramps eased faster after a small drink of pickle juice than after water. The relief came too quickly for the salt to have been absorbed, so researchers think the sour taste of vinegar triggers a reflex that calms the cramping muscle. That means it may help a cramp, but it doesn't show that pickle juice rehydrates you quickly.

**Do pickleback shots prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that they do. A pickleback is a shot of whiskey chased with pickle brine, and the small amount of brine doesn't offset the alcohol in the shot. Count picklebacks as drinks like any other and alternate with water.

**Should I drink pickle juice before bed after drinking?**

A small amount of brine with a large glass of water may help you hold on to some of that water overnight, but it won't change how much alcohol you drank or how well you sleep. Because it's acidic, it may worsen heartburn if you lie down soon after. Water and a light snack are the simpler choice.

**Who should avoid pickle juice?**

Skip it or ask a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, are on a low-sodium or fluid-restricted diet, take medicines that affect sodium or fluid balance, or have acid reflux. If you are vomiting repeatedly or can't keep fluids down, small sips of an oral rehydration solution are a better choice, and you should get medical help if it continues.

**Is fermented pickle juice better for a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that it is. Refrigerated, naturally fermented pickles may contain live bacterial cultures, while most shelf-stable vinegar pickles don't. Either way, the hangover-relevant part is the salt and water, and a shot of brine is too small and too brief to make a meaningful probiotic difference to how you feel the next morning.
